en: Dhātukathā 2 Niddesa 2.13.
The Thirteenth Method: Exposition of the Terms "Not Included" and "Associated with" and "Dissociated from."

Regarding those phenomena that are not included within the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) by way of inclusion in the aggregates, nor included by way of inclusion in the bases (āyatana), nor included by way of inclusion in the elements (dhātu): with how many aggregates, with how many bases, and with how many elements are those phenomena associated?
Those phenomena are associated with three aggregates;
they are associated with some [phenomena] by way of one base and one element.
With how many is it dissociated?
It is dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and ten elements;
it is dissociated from some [factors] with respect to one base and one element.
Those phenomena that are included in the sphere of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*), those phenomena that are included in the element of mental objects (*dhammadhātu*),
and those phenomena that are included in the female faculty (*itthindriya*).
Those phenomena [conditioned] by the male faculty;
those phenomena [conditioned] by the life-faculty;
those phenomena [conditioned] by name-and-form with consciousness as condition.
those phenomena that belong to the non-percipient realm … those phenomena that belong to the one-aggregate realm … those phenomena that belong to birth …
Those states that, by way of aging … or by way of death,
are not included in the aggregate-grouping, not included in the base-grouping, and not included in the element-grouping … [and so on] … those states are associated with three aggregates.
It is associated with one base and one element.
With how many is it dissociated?
It is dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and ten elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
Those phenomena that belong to the formless existence (arūpabhava) … those phenomena that belong to the neither-perception-nor-non-perception existence (nevasaññānāsaññābhava) …

Regarding those phenomena that belong to the fourfold existence (*catuvokārabhava*)—those phenomena which are not included in the aggregate-inclusion (*khandha-saṅgaha*), not included in the base-inclusion (*āyatana-saṅgaha*), and not included in the element-inclusion (*dhātu-saṅgaha*) by way of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*): with how many aggregates, with how many bases, and with how many elements are those phenomena associated?
There are none.
With how many is it dissociated?
It is dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements;
it is dissociated from some [factors] with respect to one base and one element.
13.1. The triads:
those states that [arise] with wholesome states … those states that [arise] with unwholesome states … [and so forth].
Those phenomena associated with pleasant feeling;
those phenomena associated with painful feeling;
those phenomena associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Those phenomena which [arise] with resultant phenomena as their condition...
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena subject to resultancy as their condition...
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena that are neither clung-to nor conducive to clinging as their condition...
Those phenomena that [arise] from defiled and defiling phenomena...
those phenomena that [arise] from undefiled and non-defiling phenomena...
those phenomena that [arise] from phenomena accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought...
Those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena that are without applied thought but possess sustained thought...
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena accompanied by rapture...
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena accompanied by pleasure...
Those phenomena which [arise] with states accompanied by equanimity...
those phenomena which [arise] with states to be abandoned by vision...
those phenomena which [arise] with states to be abandoned by cultivation...
Those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena whose causes are to be abandoned by vision...
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena whose causes are to be abandoned by cultivation...
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena leading to accumulation...
Those phenomena which, compared to the phenomena leading to diminution...
those phenomena which, compared to the phenomena of the trainee (sekha)...
those phenomena which, compared to the phenomena of the one beyond training (asekha)...
Those states [conditioned] by sublime states;
those states [conditioned] by immeasurable states;
those states [conditioned] by limited objects.
Those states which [arise] through states with exalted objects;
those states which [arise] through states with immeasurable objects; ...
those states which [arise] through inferior states.
Those phenomena which [are associated] with sublime phenomena...
those phenomena which [are associated] with phenomena fixed in falsehood...
those phenomena which [are associated] with phenomena fixed in rightness...
Those phenomena which [arise] through phenomena that have the Path as their object;
those phenomena which [arise] through phenomena that have the Path as their cause;
those phenomena which [arise] through phenomena that have the Path as their predominance.
Those phenomena which [arise] with past objects as their objective support;
those phenomena which [arise] with future objects as their objective support;
those phenomena which [arise] with present objects as their objective support.
Those phenomena [arisen] from phenomena with internal objects;
those phenomena [arisen] from phenomena with external objects;
those phenomena [arisen] from phenomena with both internal and external objects.
The Group on Causes (Hetugocchaka) Those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena that have a cause...
Those phenomena that [arise] with phenomena associated with roots;
those phenomena that [arise] with phenomena that possess roots but are not themselves roots;
and those phenomena that [arise] with phenomena that are both associated with roots and are not themselves roots.
Regarding those phenomena that are neither caused nor causeless, which are not included within the aggregates, not included within the bases,
and not included within the elements— by how many aggregates, by how many bases, and by how many elements are those phenomena associated?
There is none.
With how many is it dissociated?
It is dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element, and from some [others].
2.13.2.2–9. *Cūḷantaraduka* etc.:
Those phenomena which, among material phenomena, are not included in the aggregate-classification, not included in the base-classification, and not included in the element-classification …
Those states are associated with three aggregates;
they are associated with one base and one element by some [factors].
With how many are they dissociated?
They are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and ten elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element with respect to some [factors].
Those factors which are dissociated from immaterial phenomena...
Those phenomena that [arise] with supramundane phenomena...
those phenomena that [arise] with taintless phenomena...
those phenomena that [arise] with phenomena associated with the taints...
Those phenomena which [arise] with states associated with the taints but are not themselves taints;
those phenomena which [arise] with states dissociated from the taints and are themselves without taints;
those phenomena which are not conducive to fetters.
Those phenomena that are not to be fettered by unfetterable phenomena;
those phenomena that are not to be overwhelmed by unoverwhelmable phenomena;
those phenomena that are not to be yoked by unyokable phenomena.
Those states which [are associated] with states that are not hindrances;
those states which [are associated] with states that are not adhered to;
those states which [are associated] with states that are associated with adherence.
With respect to those states which are dissociated from the perversions, are not adhered to, and are with objects—
those states which are not included in the aggregate classification, not included in the base classification, and not included in the element classification—
with how many aggregates, with how many bases, and with how many elements are those states associated?
There is none.
With how many is it dissociated?
It is dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
2.13.2.10. Mahantaraduka:
Those phenomena which [are associated] with phenomena that are without an object...
those phenomena that [arise] with mental states;
those phenomena that [arise] with states dissociated from mind;
those phenomena that [arise] with states associated with mind...
Those phenomena [conditioned] by mind-originated phenomena;
those phenomena [conditioned] by phenomena co-existent with mind;
those phenomena [conditioned] by phenomena that follow after mind.
Regarding those phenomena that are external phenomena...

those phenomena which, among derived phenomena, are not included in the aggregate classification, not included in the base classification, and not included in the element classification—with how many aggregates, with how many bases, and with how many elements are those phenomena associated?
Those phenomena are associated with three aggregates.
They are associated with one base (āyatana) and one element (dhātu).
With how many are they dissociated?
They are dissociated from one aggregate (khandha), ten bases, and ten elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
2.13.2.11–13. The Group on Grasping, etc.:
Those phenomena which [are dissociated] from phenomena that are not subject to grasping...
Those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena associated with clinging;
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena that are both associated with clinging and are not themselves clinging;
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena dissociated from clinging and not subject to clinging.
Those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena that are non-defiled;
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena that are undefiled;
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena associated with defilements.
Those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena that are defiled but are not themselves defilements;
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena that are associated with defilements but are not themselves defilements;
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena that are dissociated from defilements and are non-defiling.
Those states which [are associated] with states to be abandoned by vision;
those states which [are associated] with states to be abandoned by cultivation;
those states which [are associated] with states rooted in what is to be abandoned by vision...
Those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena whose causes are to be abandoned by cultivation;
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena accompanied by initial application;
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena accompanied by sustained application.
Those phenomena which [arise] with states accompanied by rapture...
those phenomena which [arise] with states associated with rapture...
those phenomena which [arise] with states associated with pleasure...
Those phenomena which [arise] with states accompanied by equanimity...
those phenomena which [arise] with states belonging to the sense sphere...
those phenomena which [arise] with states belonging to the form sphere...
Those phenomena which [arise] together with the formless-sphere phenomena;
those phenomena which [arise] together with the unconditioned phenomena;
those phenomena which [arise] together with the leading-out phenomena.

Those phenomena which, by way of inclusion of aggregates (*khandha-saṅgaha*) and inclusion of bases (*āyatana-saṅgaha*), are not included among the determined phenomena (*niyata-dhamma*), nor among the unsurpassed phenomena (*anuttara-dhamma*), nor among the secure phenomena (*saraṇa-dhamma*).

Those states not included by way of inclusion in the elements (dhātu): with how many aggregates (khandha), with how many bases (āyatana), and with how many elements (dhātu) are they associated (sampayutta)?
None. With how many are they dissociated (vippayutta)?
They are dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element by some [factors].
These are the aggregate of form, the base of mental phenomena, and the element of mental phenomena.
Femininity, masculinity, life, and mind-and-form;
the two types of existence, birth, aging, and the form of death;
these are without an object and are dissociated from consciousness.
Intermingled, originating together, co-existent, following along,
external, and dependent—
these two objects are the methods of seeking for one of great wisdom. [22]
The thirteenth chapter: The Exposition of the Terms "Associated" and "Dissociated" with Respect to the Uncomprised.
